question: A product has two frontend teams, a single React app, and frequent merge conflicts because features import each other's internals. What is the best next step?
options: Split the app into micro-frontends so each team deploys alone
Turn it into a modular monolith: domain modules with public APIs, boundary checks in CI and ownership per module
Move to a monorepo with one package per component
Rewrite the app in a framework with better isolation
explanation: The pain is missing boundaries, not a shared deploy. A modular monolith adds explicit module APIs and automated rules at almost no runtime cost. Micro-frontends would turn the same tangled imports into tangled runtime contracts.

question: What does Conway's law predict for an organization of four teams working in one undivided frontend codebase?
options: The code will naturally split into four clean modules
Performance will degrade linearly with the number of teams
The code structure will reflect how the teams actually communicate, so without deliberate boundaries it becomes one tangled system
Each team will end up choosing a different framework
explanation: Systems mirror communication structures. If nothing in the code defines ownership and boundaries, everyone touches everything and the codebase mirrors that. The inverse Conway maneuver designs the boundaries first.

question: Which situation is the strongest signal that micro-frontends are justified?
options: The bundle is too large
The team wants to try a new framework on one page
Several autonomous teams own decoupled domains and are repeatedly blocked by a shared release train
The app has more than 200 components
explanation: Micro-frontends buy independent deploys for independent teams. Bundle size is solved with code splitting, component count with modules, and framework experiments rarely justify the permanent cost of distributed composition.

question: Three micro-frontends must always be released together because they share a global Redux store and import each other's components from the build output. What is this?
options: A healthy modular monolith
A distributed monolith: all the operational cost of separate deploys with none of the independence
Build-time composition, which is the recommended approach
A monorepo
explanation: Independent deployables that cannot be deployed independently are a distributed monolith. Shared mutable state and internal imports across apps are the classic causes.

question: What does adopting a monorepo with Nx or Turborepo give you on its own?
options: Independent runtime deploys for every team
Shared tooling, internal packages and affected-only, cached builds in one repository; boundaries and independent deploys still have to be designed
Automatic module boundaries
Isolation of runtime errors between apps
explanation: A monorepo is about code sharing and build orchestration. Without package boundaries it is a bigger monolith, and deploys are only independent if you build separate deployables.

question: A company splits its frontend into a 'header app', a 'forms app' and a 'tables app'. Every new feature now needs changes in all three. What went wrong?
options: They should have used iframes
They split along technical layers instead of business domains, so features cross every boundary
They needed more micro-frontends
Nothing; cross-app changes are normal
explanation: Boundaries should follow domains (catalog, checkout, account) so most features stay inside one team's app. Technical-layer splits maximize coordination, the opposite of the goal.
